# Active Work — monokl

## Completed

### SPEC-004 correction: `rust-version`/`license` fixed for michi adoption

Post-gate, post-implementation correction via `canon/correct`, triggered by the michi
integration research below. Two of AC-020's nine locked `[workspace.package]` values were
wrong: `license = "MIT"` (the repo's actual `LICENSE` file was already AGPL-3.0 — an
internal inconsistency in the source doc, unrelated to michi) and `rust-version = "1.85"`
(michi, now a confirmed dependency, needs 1.96). Corrected to `AGPL-3.0-or-later` / `1.96`,
an intentional, explicitly-flagged divergence from `docs/spec/01-core-architecture.md`'s
own literal text — canon-verifier confirmed the source document genuinely still says the
old values, so this isn't silently drifting from spec, it's a stated, gated exception.
canon-auditor caught the correction's own blast radius: the `scope` field's blanket "all
verbatim per Section 28" claim wasn't updated alongside AC-020, so it briefly contradicted
the criterion it was supposed to summarize — fixed. `vector-planner` amended `PLAN-004`
(only T-001 owns AC-020) and, checking for incidental damage, found two more:
`T-006`/`T-023` had hardcoded `rust_version=='1.85'`/`license=='MIT'` assertions baked into
otherwise-unrelated `cargo metadata` checks — not their own criteria, but would have
produced false failures on any future re-run. Fixed both. `vector-challenger`'s review of
the amended T-001 found real shell bugs of its own: the primary "nothing else moved" diff
was guaranteed to fail (comparing against a 14-line expectation when the real file already
had 67 lines of later tasks' content committed), its offered fallback was an elided `...`
wrapped around a `head | diff -` construct that starves `diff` of a second operand, and a
dangling reference told the implementer to fall back to "T-001's original pre-amendment
steps" — which no longer existed in the plan at all. All fixed, each fix independently
executed against the real repo before trusting it. `lambda-implementer` re-ran the
corrected T-001 clean — commit `414225b`.

### SPEC-004: IMPLEMENTED — the Rust crate now actually exists

First track to move past the spec@1 stage into real code. `vector-planner` produced a 23-task
plan@1 (`PLAN-004.json`); two independent `vector-challenger` rounds found and fixed 13 issues
total (three tasks whose "red" phase could never actually be red, which would have halted
`lambda-implementer` outright; a verification gap where the plan's biggest blocks of transcribed
content — the 10 later dependency version pins and all of `lib.rs` — were never diffed against
the source document, only counted; a BSD `wc -l` padding bug in a length guard my own fix
introduced; a broken backtick-in-markdown assertion; a missing cwd anchor). Third round: clean
pass.

`lambda-recon` → 23 `lambda-implementer` task dispatches (one per task, strict no-batching) →
`lambda-mutator` → `lambda-exit-gate`, all in sequence. Root `Cargo.toml`, `crates/monokl/Cargo.toml`,
and `crates/monokl/src/lib.rs` now exist and are byte-exact against `docs/spec/01-core-architecture.md`,
confirmed via pattern-anchored diffs (not hardcoded line ranges) with working length guards.
23 commits (16 file-changing, 7 deliberate `--allow-empty` for behavioral-only verification
tasks), all 28 acceptance criteria evidenced, `lambda-exit-gate` independently re-ran the
load-bearing checks against live `cargo 1.96.0` rather than trusting task reports. `lambda-mutator`
confirmed zero mutable code paths (expected — `lib.rs` is bare module declarations, no function
bodies; both `Cargo.toml`s are non-code TOML) by isolating `lib.rs` into a synthetic crate and
running `cargo mutants --list` against it (0 candidates), not by assuming the tool had nothing to do.

**Known, deliberate, already-locked gap (AC-008B): the real workspace cannot `cargo build`/`cargo test` yet.**
`io-errors` (a dependency `MonoklError` needs) is pinned to a private registry (`registry =
"orin-cargo"`) with no `.cargo/config.toml` anywhere in the corpus configuring where that registry
actually is — `cargo metadata` fails at manifest-parse time with `registry index was not found in
any configuration: \`orin-cargo\``, confirmed and locked as expected behavior by SPEC-004's own
AC-008B and re-confirmed independently by `lambda-exit-gate`. This was fine for SPEC-004 itself
(a pure manifest/module-declaration lock, verified via content-exactness diffs and isolated `/tmp`
fixtures rather than real builds) — it stops being fine the moment real Rust logic needs to
actually compile and run its own tests, which is every track from here on.

### SPEC-008: Workspace/extract config types (Track 5c) — GATED after the longest correction sequence of any track so far

Spec: `.claude/specs/SPEC-008.json` (13 acceptance criteria — `TsconfigMode`, `WorkspaceOptions`
(with its 2-method `impl` block), `ExtractRequest`). Smallest type-count of any track (3 types)
but the most exit-gate rounds: grounding and audit passes were clean (one accurate prose
correction — a citation-history overstatement claiming finding #23 had been cited elsewhere when
it hadn't), but canon-exit-gate failed **5 times** across two distinct defect classes:

**Technical precision** (2 failures) — AC-012 initially quoted serde_json's generic "expected a
string" for a wrong-type `file` value, when `camino`'s own custom `Deserialize` impl for
`Utf8PathBuf` produces "expected a UTF-8 path string" instead; and AC-009 asserted a two-class
negative/non-integral numeric-rejection rule when the real rule (established for the structurally
identical `SearchLimits` fields in SPEC-007 AC-006) is three classes, including a parse-time
"number out of range" case for magnitudes exceeding finite f64 range.

**False comparative claims** (3 failures, escalated to the human) — after retry 3 formally
exhausted canon's retry budget on an AC-010 claim that CodeBlock's own analogous
line_start/line_end gap has "no documented downstream consequence" (false: SPEC-006 AC-004
documents one, a defended-against underflow panic), the user authorized continuing past the
budget. The fix held, but two more rounds surfaced further false "unlike"/"first" claims: AC-001's
"unlike every other enum this project's specs have locked so far" (false — SPEC-005 already locks
mixed-variant enums), and after a first correction attempt replaced it with an equally false
narrower claim (citing DependencyTarget and LangData as mixed enums when neither is, and claiming
TsconfigMode is "this project's first data-carrying enum with no serde derive" when SPEC-001's
`MonoklError` already is one) — resolved per the gate's own explicit recommendation ("delete it
rather than correcting it a third time") by removing the comparative claim entirely rather than
attempting a third correction. A final, independent full-document sweep for the same pattern
found nothing further wrong, plus one purely mechanical defect (`api_surface` needed the object
shape with name/signature/description keys, not plain strings — SPEC-005's precedent).

axiom (recon → verifier → exit-gate) then surfaced one more, genuinely interesting case: 
axiom-verifier read camino/serde_core/serde_json's actual cached crate source line-by-line and
concluded AC-012's `null`-value case was wrong (predicting "unit value" instead of "null"). Before
accepting that, an actual compiled-and-run reproduction was built and checked directly — the real
output was "invalid type: null, expected a UTF-8 path string", exactly matching AC-012 as
written. axiom-verifier's static source trace had followed a code path camino's `Utf8PathBuf`
Deserialize impl doesn't actually take for a null input. axiom-exit-gate independently rebuilt the
same reproduction before issuing its verdict and confirmed: pass, high confidence, zero blockers.

Net: a good illustration of two distinct failure modes this project's rigor standard exists to
catch — the technical-precision failures are exactly why the empirical-toolchain-compilation
standard exists (a plausible-sounding claim about exact error text or class count that only a
real compile-and-run can settle); the false-comparative-claim failures are a different lesson
entirely — unverified "first"/"unlike" framing language carries zero implementable content and
was, in this track, wrong three separate times before being deleted rather than re-corrected. And
the final axiom round is the sharpest illustration yet that even *reading real crate source
line-by-line* is not a substitute for actually compiling and running it — a careful static trace
through the right crate's real code reached a confident, wrong conclusion.

### SPEC-007: Search-command request/response types (Track 5b) — GATED after an escalation to the human

Spec: `.claude/specs/SPEC-007.json` (16 acceptance criteria — `SearchOptions`, `SearchLimits`,
`Language`, `SearchResponse`, `SymbolsResult`, `DependentsResult`). Grounding pass (canon-verifier)
came back 16/16 supported, zero issues — cleanest first pass of any track so far. canon-auditor
found 5 real issues (a dangling forward-reference, two missing error cases, a missing scope
disclaimer, an untestable hypothetical-variant claim) and canon-exit-gate then failed **3
consecutive times**, every failure landing on the same criterion, AC-003 (what happens when
`SearchOptions.limits` gets a malformed JSON value): first for a false "any array length other
than 4 fails with a length error" claim (actually: >4 elements produce a `trailing characters`
error, since serde's derived `visit_seq` never drains surplus elements); then for a "for the same
reason" claim about negative-vs-non-integral rejection (actually two different serde_json error
constructors); then for a rewrite that fixed both of those but introduced a new false claim about
which array lengths hit which error class. canon-exit-gate's own retry-2 verdict formally
recommended escalating to a human rather than attempting a 4th auto-patch, correctly diagnosing
that array-form deserialize is a **short-circuiting ordered procedure** (element-type check on
positions 0..min(len,4) always runs first and can preempt the length check, regardless of the
array's actual length) — not the flat length-keyed classification every rewrite kept re-encoding.

Surfaced this to the user directly via `AskUserQuestion` rather than continuing to auto-patch.
User chose: rewrite AC-003 as the exit-gate's own confirmed ordered procedure. That rewrite
passed the ordered-procedure claim outright (survived an adversarial boundary probe: position-3
elements, length-5 arrays with only the 5th element bad, two-bad-elements-at-once), but the same
gate pass then found the numeric-literal side of the rule was only half-corrected — a genuine
**three-way** discriminator (integer within i64/u64 range; non-integer-lexical-form or
one-past-the-integer-boundary reinterpreted as floating-point; magnitude exceeding finite f64
range fails at parse time with "number out of range", naming no type at all) where the rewrite
had assumed a two-way rule "regardless of numeric value" — falsified by boundary literals
(`18446744073709551615`/`616` for u64, `-9223372036854775808`/`809` for i64, `1e308`/`1e309`).
Fixed AC-003's whole-value contract, AC-003's array-form STEP 1, and AC-006 (which had never been
updated to match and still asserted the old two-way rule, creating an intra-document
contradiction) — all three worded identically per the gate's request so they can't drift apart
again. One more round after that: STEP 1's own out-of-range clause claimed the parse-time failure
always precedes positional dispatch, refuted by two counter-examples the gate constructed
(`["a", 1e309, 3, 4]` fails at position 0's type check, not position 1's parse failure;
`[1,2,3,4,1e309]` fails with `trailing characters`, not `number out of range`, since position 4
is surplus and never parsed) — fixed to state the real rule: first failure at the lowest position
wins, whether it's a type failure or a parse failure. Final gate pass: clean, high confidence,
including a battery of adversarial cases the gate constructed itself that aren't in the criterion
text (symmetric counter-examples, position-3 boundary, position-4-is-inside-the-window checks).
Added one small zero-risk completeness item the gate flagged but didn't block on (no criterion
stated `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]`'s absence for `SearchOptions`/`SearchLimits`, unlike the
SPEC-006 precedent) before the final confirmation pass.

axiom (recon → verifier → exit-gate) then passed clean on the first attempt, 16/16 independently
re-derived rather than trusting canon's extensive history — including re-running the full AC-003
boundary-literal matrix from scratch in its own compiled crate rather than accepting canon's
result on faith.

Net: this track is the clearest demonstration yet of why the empirical-toolchain-compilation
standard exists — every one of AC-003's failures was a *plausible-sounding, wrong* claim about
serde_json's exact runtime behavior that static reading alone would not have caught, and canon's
own 3-retry escalation protocol worked exactly as designed: it recognized a pattern of
narrowing-but-still-wrong patches and routed the decision to a human rather than continuing
indefinitely.

### SPEC-006: Result/diagnostic primitives (Track 5a) — GATED, first-attempt clean on both pipelines

Spec: `.claude/specs/SPEC-006.json` (15 acceptance criteria — `CodeBlock`, `RankedBlock`,
`ParentContext`, `Diagnostic`, `DiagnosticKind`, `LineHit`). First track drafted under the
corner-case-first methodology (enumerate missing/null/wrong-type/extra-field, boundary values,

equivalence, stated precisely rather than glossed over). Also the project's first types with no

derive at all (`LineHit` — using it where `Serialize`/`Deserialize` is required is a compile-time

# Active work: monokl

`monokl search` runs end to end for TypeScript and JavaScript. Per-feature history lives in git and in `docs/spec/05-research-and-decisions.md`.

## Process

Scale ceremony to risk. The default is a short spec (about 10 criteria or fewer), tests first, `just ci`, then a normal review. Use a heavier gate chain only for a spec with real design risk or one that changes a contract other work builds on. A design decision not already in `docs/spec/05-research-and-decisions.md` goes to the owner (or `superpowers:brainstorming`) before it becomes a criterion. Record a decision that matters later as a few bullets there, with the rejected alternative. The owner merges PRs.

## Phases

| Phase | Goal | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Runnable `monokl search` | Done |
| 4 (part) | Published to crates.io, release PRs via Callisto, prebuilt binaries and Homebrew tap | Crate published; binaries in review; tap formula follows the first binary release |
| 2 | Harden | Not started |
| 3 | Rest of the commands, and speed | Not started |
| 4 (rest) | Ready to release | Not started |

Phase 2: ADR 0003 architecture test (`core` never imports `agent`, no hash maps in output types); fuzz targets (query parser, `Digest`) with a CI compile check; a capacity-limits note for the walk, parse and rank; per-shape fixture tests; the global-git-excludes test (`temp-env`); decode our TOON with the reference decoder.

Phase 3: `symbols`, `extract`; import resolution (typed outcomes) and `dependents`/`imports` with the indices; in-memory cache and `persist::v1` keyed by build; deterministic work-count tests and a benchmark.

Phase 4 (rest): semver check; README quickstart doctest; `schemaVersion` on JSON output; weekly scorecard on pinned repos; spec §1/§2/§27/§28 catch-up; optional circular-imports diagnostic via `michi-graph`.

Deferred: MCP server, michi-pipeline, napi packaging, the Rust and other-language analyzers.

## Known gaps in `monokl search`

- Diagnostics (unreadable files, the file ceiling, an exclusion-only query) are computed but never printed.
- The `extract` hint in the output points at a command that does not exist yet.

## Not built yet (design lives in `docs/spec/`)

`NodeKind`, in-memory cache, disk persistence, `WorkspaceEnricher`, indices (`FileIdx`, `ImportGraph`, `SymbolIndex`, `WorkspaceIndex`), the rest of `TsAnalyzer` (import resolution, full capability set), `symbols`/`extract`/`dependents` commands, napi FFI boundary.

## Open design questions

Each has a semantic model in `docs/architecture/` and needs a decision, not a silent port.

- **Cache corruption vs staleness recovery policy.** See `error-taxonomy.md` gap 1.
- **Cache Tier-1 content-hash gap.** The "ContentHash is authoritative" claim is not backed by the Tier-1 lookup as specified. See `cache-architecture.md`.
- **Query and ranking edge cases.** Regex hard-fail vs silent-drop is decided (hard fail). Still open: `+regex:` degradation, candidate selection above `max_candidates`, uncapped query length. See `query-and-ranking.md`.
- **Analyzer diagnostic-signal gaps.** `#[cfg]`-gated Rust code is invisible with no capability signal, and `.d.ts` files get a misleading "language unsupported" message. See `language-analyzer-contract.md`.
- **`io_safety.rs` wiring.** `read_to_string_capped` has no call sites, so `SymlinkRejected` and `FileTooLarge` cannot be constructed from any command path yet.
- **Daemon and session mode.** Future work. See `daemon-lifetimes.md`.
- **`git_scope.rs` operation tags.** Three elided sites in `collect_changes` (`03-multi-language-platform.md`) need their literal values when that module is built.

# Ranger — Cross-Language Bug Hunting

## Modes

- Full sweep: scan every hazard taxonomy.
- Targeted scan: scan the named category.
- Candidate verification: send the supplied candidate directly to adversary.
- Post-remediation check: run exit-gate against prior findings.

## Pipeline

```text
workspace → recon → scanner → [boundary-tracer] → adversary → finding-report@2 → exit-gate
```

1. `recon` records live files, entry points, languages, capabilities, workspace state, and workflow provenance in `workspace-manifest@1`.
2. `scanner` loads the matching hazard reference and emits `candidate@1` without judgment.
3. `boundary-tracer` produces `field-survival-map@1` for T7 and T10 candidates.
4. `adversary` emits `candidate-assessment@1` for one candidate. It confirms only a reachable failing scenario; external uncertainty produces `plausible`.
5. The caller aggregates findings and their families into `finding-report@2`.
6. After remediation, `exit-gate` independently derives sibling candidates and verifies current code with project-native evidence. It emits `verdict@3`.

## Defect-family route

Treat confirmed findings with the same root cause, domain responsibility, or failure state as one possible defect family. Search beyond copied syntax: equivalent behavior may use different names, control flow, or language.

When a family suggests a missing concept, state, operation, boundary, abstraction, invariant, or enforcement mechanism, pass the complete `finding-report@2` to `scribe:architect` before remediation. Local or unrelated findings remain ordinary remediation work.

## Verification depth

Choose evidence by risk, not language ritual. Use the project-native test, mutation, property, fuzz, race, integration, or boundary tools that can discriminate the suspected defect. A property or fuzz check needs a meaningful generator and oracle. Record unsupported or impractical checks as coverage gaps; do not imply coverage.

## Dispatch

| Agent | Mode | Tier | Input → output |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `recon` | Enumeration | haiku / low | workspace → `workspace-manifest@1` |
| `scanner` | Pattern matching | sonnet / medium | manifest → `candidate@1` |
| `boundary-tracer` | Data-flow tracing | sonnet / medium | T7/T10 candidate → `field-survival-map@1` |
| `adversary` | Adversarial judgment | opus / high | one candidate → `candidate-assessment@1` |
| `exit-gate` | Binding verification | opus / high | `finding-report@2` → `verdict@3` |

## Contracts

- Candidates: `shared/schemas/candidate@1.json`
- Candidate assessment: `shared/schemas/candidate-assessment@1.json`
- Workspace: `shared/schemas/workspace-manifest@1.json`
- Boundary evidence: `shared/schemas/field-survival-map@1.json`
- Findings: `shared/schemas/finding-report@2.json`
- Exit verdict: `shared/schemas/verdict@3.json`

Plausible findings pass to `flagged_for_review`; they never become remediation blockers without confirmation.

1. **Code outside top-level declarations is never returned, and nothing says so.**
   - Express `app.get(...)`, `router.use(...)`, `describe(...)`, CommonJS `module.exports = {...}`, IIFEs, top-level `if`/`for`/`try`, and un-exported `namespace` or `declare module` all produce `search: []` with exit 0.

   - A file with an unrecoverable syntax error yields nothing at all, which contradicts "searched for whatever parsed".
   - Cause: `parse.rs:124-126` visits only declaration statements, and `pipeline/mod.rs:286-291` drops hits outside every block.
2. **Diagnostics are built but never rendered.**
   - `render_projection` prints only rows, `totalCount` and hints.
   - A query with only `-term`, `--language rust`, unreadable files, parse errors and the file-ceiling warning all look identical to "nothing matched".
   - This makes #1 and several items below invisible, so I'd fix it first.
3. **`-regex:foo` does the opposite of what it says.**
   - The modifier is dropped, so `bar -regex:foo` ranks the files containing `foo` first. `+regex:fo+` becomes the literal `fo+`, and `+regex:fo(` never reaches the regex compiler.
   - Each of these exits 0. Cause: `parser.rs:82`.

## Medium
4. **The 100,000-file ceiling counts every text file.**
   - Markdown, JSON and lockfiles use it up, and the files kept are simply the first in path order.
   - A repo with 101k `.md` files returned `search: []` after 7 s, while searching `src/` alone found the match.
   - There is no truncation marker. Real trigger: `--no-ignore` in a JS repo.
5. **Budget problems.**
   - Blocks over 32 KiB are charged their byte length, so a 9k-token function can never fit the 20,000-token cap and returns nothing.
   - A top-ranked block over `--max-tokens` blanks the whole response, and the hint doesn't say a cap caused it.
   - Literal `<|endoftext|>` in source is counted as one token, which is low severity.
6. **Ranking collapses.**
   - Stop-word queries (`use`, `async`, `type`) and non-ASCII queries rank purely by path, so a re-export can outrank the function.
   - `coverage_boost` is always 1.0 (low), so it contributes nothing to ranking.
7. **`--language javascript` and `--language typescript` return the same files.**
8. **Minified one-line files keep only one function per file.** `dedup_blocks` is also quadratic: 60,000 matching files took 32 s against about 13 s linear.
9. **The published API is much wider than the product.**
   - Eight `MonoklError` variants and three `FileIoError` variants are never constructed.
   - `SearchOptions` and `SearchLimits` are unused public structs without `#[non_exhaustive]`, so changing them after a release is semver-breaking.
   - `serde_json` is a dependency only for a dead variant.
   - Every search computes symbols, dependencies, exports and a digest that are never read.

## Low
- A failed write of results (for example a full disk) still exits 0.
- The exclusion pass doubles walk time and holds every matching line in memory.
- The scan over unreadable paths is quadratic, taking 4 s at 20,000 files.
- Wildcard `_` arms violate AGENTS.md at `agent.rs:707` and `parser.rs:60`.
- A query starting with `-` needs `--`, and the README doesn't say so.
- The `extract` hint prints even when there are no rows.
- `AGENTS.md` says core types are not `Serialize`, but `SearchResponse` and `CodeBlock` derive it. ADR 0003 claims an architecture test that doesn't exist.

## Not proven
- The stack-overflow lead (hostile `.tsx` aborting the process) is still plausible and high. The nesting guard counts only `( { [`, and `catch_unwind` can't catch an overflow. The classifier stopped the stress test, so it is unrun.
- The same applies to huge-file memory, regex blowup and the lexer panic.

## Refuted
Output is deterministic (20 runs, one hash per query). Symlinks and FIFOs inside a searched tree are never read. `--max-bytes` above 2 MiB is a user override that can't enlarge the output. `--max-results 0` is truthful.

## Suggested order
1. **Fix #2** (render diagnostics), because it exposes everything else.
2. **Fix #3**, a small parser fix.
3. **Fix #1**, where a fallback block for non-declaration statements is the real design work.
4. **Fix #4 and #5**, then #6 through #9.
5. **Trim the unused API** before the next release, since it hardens once published.

- **Fixes:** do you want these as separate small PRs, with #2 and #3 first?

1	# Principles
2	
3	What monokl believes, and why. See [ARCHITECTURE.md](ARCHITECTURE.md) for how these get built.
4	
5	## Design tenets
6	
7	**Parse once, use everywhere.** A single `FileAnalysis` cache feeds every command — `search`, `symbols`, `refs`, `definition`, all of it. No command re-parses a file another command already analyzed in the same run.
8	
9	**Aggregate views, not re-scans.** The import graph and symbol index are folded from cached per-file data by `WorkspaceEnricher`s. Building workspace-wide structure never means re-walking the filesystem or re-reading files that are already cached.
10	
11	**Token budget is non-negotiable.** `max_bytes` has a hard 2MB ceiling. When output gets truncated, the response says so explicitly — a truncation marker, not silent data loss. An agent consuming monokl's output should never have to guess whether it's seeing everything.
12	
13	**Determinism.** Serialized output uses `BTreeMap` for stable key order. Ties break on `(file, line_start)`. BM25 scores round to 6 decimal places specifically to eliminate floating-point divergence between x86-64 and ARM64 — the same query against the same code should produce byte-identical JSON regardless of what machine ran it.
14	
15	**Arena lifetime containment.** No AST node born from the parser's `Allocator` escapes a per-file `analyze()` call. Every field on `FileAnalysis` is owned. This isn't a style preference — it's what makes caching and cross-thread sharing possible at all.
16	
17	**Graceful degradation.** A broken file sets `had_parse_errors = true` and still contributes whatever data survived — it doesn't abort the whole operation. An unsupported language emits a `Skipped` diagnostic — it doesn't crash or silently return nothing.
18	
19	**Tier separation.** Level 1 (`LanguageAnalyzer`, per-file) produces. Level 2 (`WorkspaceEnricher`, per-workspace) folds. Neither layer does the other's job.
20	
21	**Content hash is authoritative.** `blake3` over file content is the real cache key. `mtime`/ `size` is the cheap fast-path check that avoids reading files that haven't changed — never the source of truth on its own.
22	
23	## Non-goals
24	
25	Deliberately not built, and why:
26	
27	- **A persistent on-disk search index** (tantivy-style). The cache remembers parses; it doesn't maintain a standing inverted index. Simpler, and the numbers so far say it's fast enough without one below ~50k files — see [`docs/spec/05-research-and-decisions.md`](docs/spec/05-research-and-decisions.md).
28	- **A full [Salsa](https://github.com/salsa-rs/salsa) incremental-computation framework.** Real precedent exists for using Salsa standalone (Astral's `ty`, Biome), decoupled from rust-analyzer's own query set — this is an open investigation track, not a closed door.
29	- **Embedding-based retrieval by default.** No code-specific evidence it beats lexical + structural signals for single-codebase search, and it would mean either bundling a model or calling a cloud API — both in tension with staying local-first and low-latency. Gate behind an explicit opt-in if it's ever added; don't make it the default posture.
30	- **Stemming.** Code identifiers aren't prose; stemming rules built for English text don't transfer.
31	- **An in-memory trigram index.** Tried, measured, rejected — 600MB–1.2GB resident at scale in an earlier design. The current `WorkspaceIndex` design lands at roughly 90–140MB at 50k files by comparison.
32	- **Tree-sitter for TypeScript/JavaScript.** OXC is the native, arena-owned, actively-maintained alternative already chosen — no reason to trade that for a generic multi-language parser framework on the one language that has a better option.
33	- **A running agent loop.** monokl is a tool an agent calls, not an agent itself.
34	
35	## Language coverage isn't uniform, and shouldn't pretend to be
36	
37	A language gets a native parser and full `Structural`/`Exact` precision when it earns that investment — not by default, and not on a fixed roadmap regardless of what the parser ecosystem actually supports.
38	
39	- **TypeScript/JS and Rust** — real, mature native-Rust parsers (OXC, `ra_ap_syntax`).
40	- **Python and Java** — no viable native option exists, checked directly against crates.io, so they use tree-sitter instead.
41	- **Go** — `gosyn` is a real, actively-maintained native option.
42	
43	Precision targets follow from what's achievable per language, declared explicitly via the `CapabilityPrecision` model — never silently assumed uniform across languages that aren't.
44

Not well enough. Measured against its own stated principles, the shipped `monokl search` breaks several. I'd also say the project has been optimising for architecture rather than for the goal.

**The goal** (README and `PRINCIPLES.md`): an agent should get the right code, in as few tokens as possible, without guessing whether it's seeing everything.

**Where the audit says we fall short of that:**
- *"Graceful degradation … doesn't silently return nothing."* We silently return nothing for Express routes, `describe` blocks, CommonJS modules, scripts, files with syntax errors, and unsupported languages.
- *"An agent should never have to guess whether it's seeing everything."* The file ceiling, the budget cut and dropped diagnostics all produce output that looks complete.
- *Token efficiency.* A method hit returns the whole class, which costs more context than a grep hit would.
- *Determinism* holds, and it's the one tenet we've tested properly.

**The direction problem:** most of the work went into things the shipped command doesn't use. That includes the symbol/dependency/export extraction computed on every search but never read, the daemon and cache designs, the multi-language types, and the git/cache/symlink error variants. Meanwhile nobody has measured whether `monokl search` beats `rg` for an agent. The BM25 constants are, by the spec's own admission, unvalidated, and my earlier competitive notes already recommended an eval harness. Those notes also named Express/route enrichment as high value, and the tool can't find route handlers at all today.

I haven't measured the goal either. This judgment comes from reading the code and the audit, not from benchmarks.

**What I'd do instead of phase 3 as planned:**
1. Fix the tenet violations in `search`: render diagnostics, fix `-regex:`, and cover the non-declaration code that grep finds and we don't. Those are the first three audit items.
2. Build a small eval before more commands. About 20 real queries across 3 repos, scoring monokl against `rg` on "right code found" and tokens consumed. A day of work, and it tells us whether the ranking is worth anything.
3. Hold `symbols`, `extract`, the cache and the daemon until the eval says search is worth building on. Stop computing unused analysis data on every search.
4. Trim the published API surface before the next release.

One question decides a lot: is the target an agent-facing search that beats grep on token cost, or the broader code-intelligence platform the specs describe? The current plan quietly assumes the second, and I'd rather you chose than that we drift into it.
Let's consider that goal and redo the adversarial analaysis right?

Yes. This time the question changes from "where is it buggy" to "for an agent doing real tasks, does monokl beat `rg` on finding the right code per token?". First I need to know which TypeScript repos are on this machine to use as a corpus.

What trails are:

input.content:
Removes `rust-toolchain.toml`, which put every PR's CI on Rust 1.99.0 instead of the pinned 1.98.1.

- **Cause.** #31 added `rust-toolchain.toml` with `channel = "stable"`. `.prototools` pins Rust at 1.98.1 and CI installs that version, but cargo prefers the repo file, so clippy 1.99.0 ran. Its new lints (`assert_is_empty` in tests, and `float_cmp` expectations that no longer fire) fail `-D warnings` in unchanged code.
- **Why it's still here.** #31 merged without the follow-up commit that removed the file, so `main` has it. That is why Lint fails on #35 and the Dependabot PRs.
- **Fix.** Delete the file. The pin in `.prototools` stays the single source of truth.

After this merges, the open PRs need a rebase (`@dependabot rebase` on the Dependabot ones) to pick it up.

A bump to 1.99 needs the ~11 lint fixes in tests and should be made on purpose, by changing `.prototools`.

# brew tap-new uses this file to generate an autobump workflow for the new tap
name: brew bump

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
    paths:
      - .github/workflows/autobump.yml
  workflow_dispatch:
  schedule:
    # Every day at 15:35 UTC
    - cron: 35 15 * * *

permissions: {}

defaults:
  run:
    shell: bash -xeuo pipefail {0}

jobs:
  autobump:
    if: github.repository == 'orin-dx/homebrew-tap'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      - name: Set up Homebrew
        id: set-up-homebrew
        uses: Homebrew/actions/setup-homebrew@d482da0e602890d3160aade42e72c8556103bf04 # 2026.10.26.1

      - name: Set up git
        id: git_setup
        uses: Homebrew/actions/git-user-config@d482da0e602890d3160aade42e72c8556103bf04 # 2026.10.26.1

      # PRs opened with the default GITHUB_TOKEN do not trigger the test-bot workflow.
      - name: Create tap-scoped GitHub App token
        id: app-token
        uses: actions/create-github-app-token@64ab729a6294000f5aa4a4bc0b73d1f32bc45510 # v3
        with:
          client-id: ${{ vars.TAP_APP_CLIENT_ID }}
          private-key: ${{ secrets.TAP_APP_PRIVATE_KEY }}
          owner: orin-dx
          repositories: homebrew-tap
          permission-contents: write
          permission-pull-requests: write

      # A bump that crosses into a new breaking line must keep the old line installable, so open that
      # snapshot PR first. The merge workflow holds the bump PR until the snapshot is on main.
      - name: Open snapshot PRs for new breaking lines
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ steps.app-token.outputs.token }}
          TAP_NAME: ${{ steps.set-up-homebrew.outputs.tap-name }}
        run: |
          tap_dir=$(brew --repository "$TAP_NAME")
          brew livecheck --json --newer-only --tap="$TAP_NAME" > "$RUNNER_TEMP/livecheck.json"
          python3 "$tap_dir/.github/scripts/tap_automation.py" snapshot \
            --repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" --tap-dir "$tap_dir" --livecheck "$RUNNER_TEMP/livecheck.json"

      - name: Bump formulae
        env:
          HOMEBREW_GITHUB_API_TOKEN: ${{ steps.app-token.outputs.token }}
          HOMEBREW_GIT_COMMITTER_NAME: ${{ steps.git_setup.outputs.name }}
          HOMEBREW_GIT_COMMITTER_EMAIL: ${{ steps.git_setup.outputs.email }}
          TAP_NAME: ${{ steps.set-up-homebrew.outputs.tap-name }}
        run: brew bump --no-fork --open-pr --formulae --bump-synced --tap="$TAP_NAME"
# How tap updates work

The tap follows tagged releases. It does not decide when Callisto or Caliper publishes, and a release workflow does not write a formula directly. The three workflows are the ones `brew tap-new` generates, with a few additions noted below.

## The path from release to bottles

1. **Detect.** The **brew bump** workflow (`autobump.yml`) runs daily, or on demand. It runs `brew bump --open-pr`, which asks each formula's `livecheck` block for the newest stable tag and opens a PR that changes the source `url` and `sha256`. Versioned formulae such as `callisto@0.15` follow patch releases of their own line only, because their `livecheck` regex is pinned to it. Before it bumps, the workflow checks whether a tool is crossing into a new breaking line (a new minor before 1.0, a new major after). If so, and no `tool@line` formula exists yet, it opens a snapshot PR that keeps the old line installable. The source repositories need no tap-specific workflow or secret.
2. **Test.** **brew test-bot** (`tests.yml`) styles and audits the tap, then builds, tests, and bottles each changed formula on macOS ARM and Linux ARM and x86-64. A final step fails the job if a changed formula produced no bottle, because test-bot can skip a formula and still pass. Intel macOS is unsupported: Homebrew publishes no Intel bottles, so `rust` cannot be installed there without a source build, and the formulae use `disable!` to stop with a clear message. Bottles are uploaded as workflow artifacts.
3. **Merge.** The release was already reviewed in the parent repository, so the updater App's PRs do not wait for a second approval. The **merge release bumps** workflow (`automerge.yml`) merges one when the three platform checks passed on its head commit and every guard in `.github/scripts/tap_automation.py` holds: the PR comes from the App on a branch in this repository, it changes only `Formula/*.rb`, only the source `url` and `sha256` change (or it adds the exact snapshot the script generates), the URL stays in the same upstream repository, the version goes up, and a bump into a new line waits until the old line's formula is on `main`. A PR that fails a guard stays open for a human to review. The workflow runs after test-bot, after every push to `main` (a merged snapshot unblocks its bump), and every six hours. If a PR sits unmerged for a day, it opens an issue. Human-authored and Dependabot PRs still need a maintainer's review.
4. **Publish.** When the PR merges, **brew pr-pull** (`publish.yml`) runs on its own. It runs `brew pr-pull --no-cherry-pick`, which downloads the bottles built for that PR, uploads them, and adds the `bottle do` block to the formula. Because the PR is already merged, the workflow passes brew the commit the PR merged onto, so brew can tell which formulae changed, and runs with `--clean` so it never amends a commit already on `main`. It then attests build provenance and pushes the bottle commit to `main`. Only merged PRs from this repository that change `Formula/` trigger it, and it runs the base branch's workflow code, so a PR cannot alter what runs with the App token. Afterwards it installs each published formula on macOS ARM and Linux ARM and x86-64 and fails unless Homebrew pours a bottle. If publishing or that check fails, it opens an issue.

The URL comes from the formula and the tag from `livecheck`; `brew bump` computes the checksum itself.

## One-time GitHub setup

### Create the App

Pull requests opened with the default `GITHUB_TOKEN` do not trigger other workflows, so the bump workflow uses a short-lived GitHub App token instead. The publish workflow uses the same App to push the bottle commit to `main`, and the merge workflow uses it to merge the App's own PRs. Create an organization-owned GitHub App called something like `orin-dx-homebrew-updater`. Disable its webhook. Give it only **Contents: read and write** and **Pull requests: read and write**, then install it on **only `orin-dx/homebrew-tap`**.

Generate one private key and record the App's client ID. Keep the PEM out of Git and terminal output. Store them as an Actions variable and secret that only `homebrew-tap` can read. Repository-level is simplest:

```sh
gh variable set TAP_APP_CLIENT_ID -R orin-dx/homebrew-tap
gh secret set TAP_APP_PRIVATE_KEY -R orin-dx/homebrew-tap < path/to/downloaded-key.pem
```

An organization-level variable and secret work too if their repository access is limited to `homebrew-tap`; this tap uses that form. The variable command prompts for the client ID. The secret command reads the PEM from stdin; delete the downloaded file after storing it. No other repository needs the key, and because the App bypasses the `main` ruleset, no other repository should be able to read it.

### Protect `main`

Add a repository ruleset for `main`: require a PR, one approval, dismiss stale approvals after new pushes, and require the three **brew test-bot** jobs: `macOS ARM`, `Linux x86-64`, and `Linux ARM`. Add the App to the ruleset's bypass list with **Always allow**. That bypass is how the publish workflow pushes the bottle commit, which Homebrew's bottle model needs on `main` after the PR merges, and how the merge workflow merges the App's PRs without a second approval. The bypass also skips the required checks, so the merge workflow waits for them itself and refuses to merge anything that fails its guards. The App's token is minted only in the bump, merge, and publish workflows, and the publish workflow runs only for merged PRs from this repository. Repository admins and the maintainer account are also on the bypass list for human-authored maintenance. Leave automatic merge off.

### Bottle storage

Bottles are stored as assets on GitHub Releases in this repository, one release per formula version (for example `caliper-0.7.0`). `test-bot` writes that `root_url` into each bottle, and `brew pr-upload` creates the release and uploads the assets with the App token's Contents write permission. No package permissions are needed.

gh workflow run automerge.yml -R orin-dx/homebrew-tap
gh workflow run publish.yml -R orin-dx/homebrew-tap -f pull_request=<number>

content.text:
Short answer: close the notification part of #30, but not necessarily the whole PR. I checked the tap's `tap-automation` branch locally, and its formulae no longer use our release binaries.

- **Formulae build from source.** `callisto.rb` points at the GitHub source tarball of the tag, with `depends_on "rust" => :build`. The tap then builds and publishes its own Homebrew bottles from that source.
- **The tap discovers releases by itself.** `autobump.yml` runs `brew bump --open-pr` daily and on demand, using each formula's `livecheck` regex (`^monokl@…$` fits our tags). The tap's own docs say "The source repositories need no tap-specific workflow or secret."
- **So monokl needs nothing for Homebrew:** no `notify-tap` job, and no access to `TAP_APP_CLIENT_ID` or `TAP_APP_PRIVATE_KEY`. That job in #30 is dead weight, and the old dispatch path was never strictly required anyway (it also had a daily cron).

**What's left in #30 is the prebuilt binaries**, four attested archives per GitHub release. Homebrew won't use them. They'd serve `curl | tar` installs and a proto plugin, which is how callisto ships its own.

**My recommendation:**
- If you only wanted binaries for Homebrew: close #30. Nothing else in it is needed, and the README install lines would need rewording.
- If you want direct downloads and proto support: keep #30 and I'll strip the `notify-tap` job from it. That makes the release workflow simpler and safer.
- Either way, remove `monokl` from the org variable and secret's selected repos, since the key shouldn't be readable by a repo that doesn't need it.

**Two caveats:**
- The automation I read lives on the tap's unmerged branches and PRs (#13–#15). Tap `main` locally still has the older dispatch workflow, so "the tap listens for changes" only holds once those merge.
- The tap adds the new formula by its own PR, so monokl has no tap-side PR to open for it either.

Also from your earlier questions:
- **#35's failing Lint** was the stray `rust-toolchain.toml` that is still on `main`.
- **The fix is #36.** Its checks are still running, and once it merges the failing PRs need a rebase (`@dependabot rebase`).
- **Entire Gates** also failed on #33. That's a separate gate I haven't diagnosed.

The failures split into three separate causes, and only one of them is code.

**1. Lint on #32, #33 and #34: already fixed on `main`, but the PRs predate it.**
- Their runs are from before #36 merged. They need a rebase onto `main`: comment `@dependabot rebase` on each.
- #32 (`install-action` bump) and #33 (oxc group) otherwise pass everything: Test, MSRV, Coverage, Audit and Changesets. After the rebase, only Entire Gates is left for them (point 3).

**2. #34 has a real break and needs a code change.**
- It bumps `tiktoken-rs` from 0.6 to 0.12.1, which changes the API. `o200k_base_singleton()` now returns `&'static CoreBPE`, with no mutex, so `.lock()` at `budget.rs:71` fails to compile. That is why Test (macOS and Ubuntu), MSRV and Coverage all fail.
- The fix is to drop `.lock()` there, and while in that line I'd also switch to `encode_ordinary`, which the audit flagged. 0.12.0's notes also mention error-aware encoding changes, so I'd check the compile against the new signatures.
- Dependabot can't fix this itself. Commit it onto the PR branch, or open our own bump PR and close #34. A commit on the branch stops Dependabot rebasing it afterwards, which is fine because you'd merge it right after.

**3. Entire Gates fails on every Dependabot PR (not on ours).**
- I can't read the gate output from here (it's on entire.com). Your other session's candidates fit: Human Review needs approval, Up to Date, or Agent Review findings. Our own PRs show it pending, and Dependabot's show it failing.
- That is a settings decision in Entire (Settings → Gates), not code. If you want Dependabot PRs to pass without a human, relax Human Review for the Dependabot actor, or accept approving them.

**Your question about #30:** yes, it changes things. If the tap follows our releases by itself (its `brew bump` livecheck on `monokl@…` tags), then the `notify-tap` job is unnecessary, and so is monokl's access to the tap App key. What remains in #30 is the four prebuilt binaries, which Homebrew won't use because the tap builds from source and makes its own bottles. I'd keep them only for direct downloads and a proto plugin like callisto's. Otherwise close #30.
